claims.text: This is not a celiac-safe kitchen. Several of Padma's signature dishes are built on wheat: a katsudon made with kuruma-fu (wheat gluten / fu) and a wheat-gluten 'meat' substitute (seitan/fu) appear as mains, so wheat is handled and cooked throughout the kitchen.
The menu also includes fried, battered items such as tempura broccoli and a vegetable cutlet, which typically use wheat flour batter and a shared fryer - an additional gluten cross-contact risk.

No source documents the use of wheat-free tamari. As with most Japanese kitchens, assume standard soy sauce and fermented seasonings (the kitchen relies on miso and plum vinegar) may contain wheat unless confirmed with staff.
Padma is a fully plant-based kitchen - no meat, fish, eggs or dairy are used anywhere - so the risk of animal-product cross-contact is minimal. The menu is explicitly vegan/oriental-vegetarian.
Even desserts are animal-free, e.g. macrobiotic sweets such as blueberry amazake pudding rather than dairy-based items.

The owner describes cooking that adapts to the individual - serving gentler meals for guests avoiding raw foods, reducing salt, or with particular health needs - which suggests she is willing to accommodate requests, though no formal allergy protocol is documented.
100% plant-based menu, so vegan diners can order freely without checking for hidden animal ingredients.

Ingredient-conscious cooking: organic, pesticide-free Kyoto vegetables, brown rice, and deliberately simple recipes the owner says a guest can understand when they ask how a dish is made - helpful when discussing what's in your food.

name: 京料理 万長 (Kyoto Cuisine Mancho)

claims.text: This is traditional Kyoto cuisine served as multi-course bento and kaiseki, where soy sauce, dashi, and other wheat-containing seasonings are used throughout. It should not be considered celiac-safe, and there is no documented gluten-free preparation or guarantee.

Tempura is a regular part of the menu (seasonal vegetable, bamboo shoot, and rape blossom tempura are highlighted in guest accounts), so a wheat-flour batter and likely shared fryer are present in the kitchen. No dedicated gluten-free fryer is documented.

As with most Japanese kitchens, the soy sauce used here can be expected to contain wheat, and it features across the seasonal dishes. Diners avoiding gluten should treat the menu as containing wheat unless staff confirm otherwise.

Dishes are built on Japanese dashi (typically made with bonito and/or other fish) and are not vegan or vegetarian by default. No plant-based or vegan menu is documented; vegan diners would need to arrange a custom course directly with the restaurant.

Manchō prepares set bento and kaiseki courses and caters to a range of occasions, so the kitchen is accustomed to working from advance orders. Guests with dietary needs are best served by phoning ahead to discuss what can be accommodated.
Entire kitchen is free-from — no wheat, gluten, egg or dairy used anywhere, so celiac cross-contamination risk is inherently minimal. Pasta is gluten-free ('もちろんパスタはグルテンフリー') and bread is rice-flour.
The inherited wood-fired pizza oven remains but is 'not currently in use' (今のところ使用されていない), so no wheat flour is handled for pizza.
Kitchen uses no egg or dairy at all; plant-based probiotic gelato (植物性乳酸菌のジェラート) is offered as a dessert.
Tabelog advises guests with allergies to state them when booking; the owner-chef built the restaurant specifically for allergy sufferers.
Celiac blogger mamehana praised the pasta as tasting authentically like real pasta, unlike ordinary commercial gluten-free pasta, and confirmed the whole restaurant is 小麦・グルテン・卵・乳製品不使用.
Purpose-built allergy-adapted Italian: no wheat/gluten/egg/dairy on the entire menu, corn+rice pasta, 米粉 bread.
The tare is built on a special soy sauce, which in Japan is standard wheat-brewed shoyu; combined with wheat noodles this bowl is not gluten-free.
Every bowl is finished with pork-belly chashu and shares a counter kitchen with meat and egg toppings, so no plant-only preparation is offered.

name: 油そば ねこまた (Abura Soba Nekomata)

claims.text: Abura soba is fundamentally a wheat-noodle dish in a soy/wheat-based tare; no gluten-free handling is published.
The tare is described as a soy-sauce (醤油) based seasoning, which in Japan is virtually always wheat-containing shoyu.
Standard bowls include pork chashu and an onsen-egg topping; no vegan/vegetarian version is advertised.
English menu available, easing communication for non-Japanese-speaking diners.

name: 油そば専門店 ムジコ (Abura Soba Senmonten Mujiko)

claims.text: The abura soba is dressed with a special soy-sauce-based tare (特製醤油ダレ); Japanese soy sauce typically contains wheat, and no wheat-free/tamari alternative is mentioned.
Flavor bases include pork and seafood (fish/niboshi dried-sardine) broths and oils, so the noodles are not vegan even before the soy tare.

name: 油そば・まぜそば ロマン 百万遍店 (Aburasoba・Mazesoba Roman Hyakumanben-ten)

claims.text: The kitchen centers on house-made whole-wheat thick noodles boiled in shared water, so wheat cross-contact is unavoidable throughout.
Both signature bowls are dressed with a special shoyu (soy sauce) tare, which is wheat-based and a core component of the dish.
Bowls include chashu pork, spicy minced meat, and egg, with shared utensils and prep surfaces; no plant-based preparation is offered.

name: あいつのラーメン かたぐるま 本店 (Aitsu no Ramen Kataguruma Honten)

claims.text: Wheat noodles, wheat-containing tare (salt and soy/pork-bone bases), and shared broth pots mean gluten is pervasive; no separate gluten-free handling is indicated.
Evening menu shifts to soy/pork-bone (醤油系) variations; ramen shoyu tare in Japan is standardly wheat-based.
All bowls are built on pork-bone/chicken/fish broth and topped with chashu; no vegan preparation exists, so cross-contact with animal products is unavoidable.
